50 sibling pairs, one sibling with DSM-IV stimulant dependence and the other with no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse, against 50 unrelated volunteers matched for age and IQ. Both siblings had lower white-matter fractional anisotropy than the volunteers (tract skeleton, F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001), and it was more alike within true sibling pairs than within random pairs (permutation P = 0.004). Three grey-matter clusters were shared by both sibling groups: a larger left amygdala and left putamen, and a smaller left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula; the putamen (P = 0.013) and posterior insula (P = 0.012) differences were familial by the permutation test, the amygdala difference was not (P = 0.144). The main report names no hippocampal, orbitofrontal or anterior insular difference, reports no direct comparison of the two siblings and does not say which stimulants were used; the supplement, which holds the cluster statistics and the sample characteristics, was not read.

In one study of 50 sibling pairs, in each of which one sibling met DSM-IV criteria for stimulant dependence and the other had no history of chronic drug or alcohol abuse (the paper's criterion), both siblings had lower white-matter fractional anisotropy than 50 unrelated controls matched for age and IQ, and shared three grey-matter clusters of difference from them: a larger left amygdala, a larger left putamen, and smaller volume across the left postcentral gyrus, superior temporal gyrus and posterior insula. The white-matter, putamen and posterior insula differences were more alike within families than between unrelated people; the amygdala difference was not. The main report names no hippocampal difference (it reports a larger medial temporal lobe, with the left amygdala as the shared cluster), no orbitofrontal or anterior insular difference, and no direct comparison of the two siblings; a review describes a larger hippocampus in both siblings and smaller orbitofrontal and anterior insular volumes in the dependent siblings only, which may come from the paper's supplement, not yet read.

set.plain: Brothers and sisters of people dependent on stimulants, who had no history of long-term drug or alcohol problems themselves, shared some of the same brain differences from unrelated volunteers. That suggests some differences run in families and may come before drug use, although nobody was scanned before they started using. In the dependent person, some differences were larger the longer they had used stimulants, which suggests the drug use may add to them. A review reports other differences found only in the dependent person, but the study's main report does not name or test them. Most of the dependent people in that study used cocaine, according to a review; it is not known whether any used meth.
set.magnitude: No standardized effect sizes or cluster statistics in the main report. Fractional anisotropy: group difference F(2,141) = 26.3, P < 0.001, which implies 144 of the 150 participants analysed (editors' calculation: η² about 0.27). Within-family similarity (permutation tests, uncorrected for multiple testing): white matter P = 0.004, putamen P = 0.013, posterior insula P = 0.012, amygdala P = 0.144 (not familial).
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high on the study card (provisional; the supplement was not read): sex, education and other drug use not reported in the main report, smoking more common in both sibling groups and checked only for grey matter, 6 of 150 participants missing from the analyses by the degrees of freedom, and only the clusters shared by both siblings described.
set.grade.reasoning: One cross-sectional study of 50 sibling pairs, read in full except its supplement. Starts low (observational). Risk of bias, one level: ROBINS-E overall high on the study card (provisional), because sex, education and other drug use are not reported in the main report, smoking was more common in both sibling groups and was checked only for grey matter, the degrees of freedom imply that 6 of 150 participants are missing from the analyses without explanation, and only the clusters shared by both siblings are described. Indirectness, one level: the main report does not name the stimulants, which according to a review were mostly cocaine. Imprecision, one level: 50 people per group, voxel-wise whole-brain tests whose correction is described only in the supplement, and familiality tests without correction for multiple testing (three of the six would not pass a Bonferroni threshold, editors' calculation). Certainty very low. The claim is rated as an association; whether the shared differences predate use cannot be settled by this design.

California inpatient and death records, 1990–2005: people aged 30 or over with a methamphetamine/amphetamine-related admission (n = 40,472), with no alcohol, other drug or HIV code at any time and no earlier parkinsonism, followed for up to 16 years for a later inpatient Parkinson's disease diagnosis (ICD-9 332.0) or death from Parkinson's disease. Matched 1:1 on age, race, sex, index date and number of later admissions to people hospitalized for appendicitis (40,358 pairs): 51 vs 29 cases, competing-risks HR 1.76 (95% CI 1.12–2.76, p = 0.014; the abstract prints 1.12–2.75 and p = 0.017); median age at diagnosis 57.2 vs 63.8 years. Against matched people with cocaine-related diagnoses (17,696 pairs): 36 vs 15 cases, HR 2.41 (1.32–4.41; the abstract prints 2.44). Cocaine against appendicitis (23,281 pairs): 20 vs 21 cases, HR 1.04 (0.56–1.93). Editors' calculation: crude proportions 0.13% vs 0.07% over a mean of about 6 years from the index admission to the end of the study.

evidence_set: Adverse effects › Methamphetamine overdose, 1st–3rd paragraphs (p. 1088) and 4th paragraph (p. 1091, after Table 3)

Based on case reports (references 29 and 44–51, several of amphetamine poisoning), the common features of overdose are agitation, dilated pupils, tachycardia, hypertension and rapid respiration; other features include shivering, dyspnoea, chest pain, hyperpyrexia and cardiac, hepatic or renal failure, and coma or seizures occur less frequently. Non-fatal toxicity presents typically with tachycardia, hypertension and altered mental status: agitation in about 20% of cases, suicidal ideation in 6–12%, acute psychosis in 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis in up to 14% and seizures in 3–4% (references 52–55: emergency-department series and a treatment trial, partly of amphetamine; no sample sizes or denominators given). Case reports attribute deaths most often to pulmonary oedema or congestion, cerebrovascular haemorrhage, ventricular fibrillation, acute cardiac failure or hyperpyrexia; forensic series (references 58–60) suggest that a significant and possibly greater proportion of methamphetamine-related deaths arise from accidents, suicide and homicide. Proposed toxic and fatal blood concentrations are guides only, because deaths and survival have been reported across overlapping ranges. No case fatality among presentations and no comparison of fatal with non-fatal cases is given. About 94 000 US emergency-department visits in 2005 were associated with recent methamphetamine use.

set.plain: Severe meth toxicity can look like a body in overdrive: agitation, wide pupils, a racing heart, high blood pressure and fast breathing. Less often there is very high body temperature, chest pain, seizures, muscle breakdown, or heart, liver or kidney failure, and some people die. This comes from a review of case reports and hospital emergency studies; the review says, for example, that seizures happened in about 3 or 4 in 100 non-fatal cases, but we have not yet checked these figures in the original studies, and some of them concern amphetamine rather than meth. The same review notes that many meth-related deaths come from accidents, suicide and homicide. Whether high body temperature predicts death has not been studied in the sources we have read.
set.magnitude: As summarized by the review (second-hand; no denominators or sample sizes): among non-fatal presentations, agitation about 20%, suicidal ideation 6–12%, acute psychosis 7–12%, rhabdomyolysis up to 14%, seizures 3–4%. Not given: case fatality among presentations, the proportion of deaths with other drugs detected, or any comparison of fatal with non-fatal cases.
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: The primary case reports and series cannot be appraised through the review (editors' narrative-review checklist on the study card: high).
set.grade.domains.indirectness.note: Second-hand through a narrative review (METHODS §6.3); some of the cited series concern amphetamine rather than methamphetamine.
set.grade.reasoning: The features and frequencies come from a narrative review (Cruickshank & Dyer, 2009), now read in full and used only as a pointer (METHODS §5.3). Its overdose section rests on case reports (several of amphetamine poisoning, from 1960 onward), a few emergency-department series and a treatment trial, and forensic series, none appraised in the review and none yet read here. Descriptive features from case series start low (relation 'describes', METHODS §6.1). Risk of bias, one level: the primary studies cannot be appraised through the review. Indirectness, one level: the figures are second-hand, and some cited series concern amphetamine rather than methamphetamine. Certainty very low. Any statement about what predicts death needs studies that compare fatal with non-fatal cases.

National Comorbidity Survey, September 1990 to February 1992: probability sample of the noninstitutionalized population aged 15–54 in the 48 coterminous states, response rate 82.4%, n = 8,098; DSM-III-R dependence by lay-administered CIDI. Of the population, 15.3% (SE 0.7) had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically (examples given: dextroamphetamine, methamphetamine) and 1.7% (SE 0.3) had ever been dependent on them, so 11.2% (SE 1.6) of those who had used them had ever met the criteria. Corresponding proportions: tobacco 31.9% (no SE; tobacco use from the 1991 NHSDA, dependence assessed for daily smoking in a subsample of 4,414), alcohol 15.4% (SE 0.7), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), cannabis 9.1% (0.7), heroin 23.1% (5.6), any controlled substance or inhalant 14.7% (0.7). Each proportion is the lifetime prevalence of dependence divided by the lifetime prevalence of use on at least one occasion. Editors' calculation: 95% CI for the stimulant proportion about 8.1% to 14.3%.
perhaps a vast majority, do not seem to make a transition to drug dependence

set.population: US household (noninstitutionalized) population aged 15–54 in 1990–1992 who had ever used psychostimulants other than cocaine extramedically
set.exposure: lifetime extramedical use of psychostimulants other than cocaine (including prescription stimulants used without or beyond a prescription)
set.magnitude: Proportion ever dependent among people who had ever used extramedically (weighted NCS estimates, n = 8,098; Table 2): psychostimulants other than cocaine 11.2% (SE 1.6; editors' 95% CI about 8.1% to 14.3%), from 15.3% lifetime use and 1.7% lifetime dependence in the population; tobacco 31.9% (no SE), alcohol 15.4% (0.7), cocaine 16.7% (1.5), cannabis 9.1% (0.7), heroin 23.1% (5.6). Stimulants by age: 13.5% (15–24), 13.9% (25–34), 7.7% (35–44), 6.5% (45–54); by sex: men 9.7%, women 13.3% (Tables 4–5).
set.grade.domains.risk_of_bias.note: JBI items met or largely met (study card, overall low): national probability sample, response 82.4% with a non-response survey and weighting, a standardized CIDI interview and design-based standard errors. The noninstitutionalized frame aged 15–54, the exclusion of people who had died and self-report could move the figure in either direction, as the authors note, but are not judged large enough to change it materially.
set.grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (a proportion in a survey population): starts low. Risk of bias not downgraded: the JBI items are met or largely met (study card; overall low); the frame, the exclusion of people who had died and self-report could move the figure in either direction, as the authors discuss (pp. 263–265), but not by enough to change it materially. Indirectness, two levels: the class is psychostimulants other than cocaine, of which methamphetamine is one example and which includes extramedical use of prescription stimulants; the criteria are DSM-III-R; the data are from 1990–1992. The tobacco proportion is less comparable than the others: it combines tobacco use from a separate 1991 survey with dependence assessed for daily smoking in a subsample, and has no standard error. Certainty very low. Included because the authors conclude from these figures that many, perhaps most, people who use a drug do not become dependent (p. 265), an observation they describe as increasingly well documented; the data support it substance by substance, and as a proportion at the interview rather than a lifetime risk.
